title: Prospect and refuge theory: Constructing a critical definition for architecture and design

findings.antecedent: Environments allowing observation without being seen (prospect and refuge)
findings.consequent: Feeling of security and meeting basic human psychological needs
findings.quote: The theory of “prospect and refuge” seeks to describe why certain environments feel secure and thereby meet basic human psychological needs. Environments that meet such needs will often provide people with the capacity to observe (prospect) without being seen (refuge).

findings.antecedent: Enclosed space
findings.quote: Kaplan (1983) maintains that an enclosed space will evoke a feeling of safety or relaxation...

findings.antecedent: View from an enclosed space
findings.quote: ...while a view from that space can add levels of stimulation and excitement.

findings.antecedent: Certain combination of spatial and formal complexity and order
findings.quote: Hildebrand (1991) also argues that a certain combination of spatial and formal complexity and order is required in order to uncover the particular prospect-refuge relationship present in domestic architecture.

findings.antecedent: Controlling how open and bright spaces are framed spatially
findings.quote: Hildebrand identifies that prospect and refuge may result intuitively in the work of an architect who seeks to control the manner in which open and bright spaces are framed spatially.

findings.antecedent: Environmental conditions favorable to biological survival
findings.quote: Appleton's first proposition, called “habitat theory”, relates pleasure to environmental conditions that are favourable to biological survival including 'the ability of a place to satisfy all our biological needs' (1975, 70).

findings.antecedent: Strategic appraisal of landscapes enabling 'ability to see without being seen'
findings.consequent: Immediate source of aesthetic satisfaction ('prospect-refuge theory')
findings.quote: Appleton's second proposition, “prospect-refuge theory”, proposed the strategic appraisal of various landscapes as potential habitats that enable “the ability to see without being seen” (73); a property which is an “immediate source of aesthetic satisfaction” (73).

findings.antecedent: Spatial arrangement, opportunity for movement/exploration, shadow/sun, and 'hazards'
findings.quote: According to Appleton, what influences the human perception of a landscape are the spatial arrangement of various components that support seeing and hiding, the opportunity for movement and exploration as well as the impact of shadow and sun.

findings.antecedent: Perceived risk observed from a secure position
findings.quote: A perceived risk that is observed from a secure position, might be tempting and exciting...

findings.antecedent: Capacity to hide in an enclosed, dark space near danger
findings.quote: ...just as the capacity to hide in an enclosed, dark space while there might be danger nearby could be regarded as a pleasurable experience.

findings.antecedent: Equal proportion of prospect, refuge, and hazard symbols
findings.quote: Appleton argues that an equal proportion of prospect, refuge and hazard symbols may establish “balance” (121) in a landscape.

findings.antecedent: 'Mystery' (suggests opportunity to venture further and learn more)
findings.quote: The Kaplans' (1983) exploration of habitat preference is, like Appleton's, a response to the combination of human needs and environmental conditions. In this work, they propose that a key factor influencing preference is “mystery”.

findings.antecedent: 'Openness in a natural scene' and 'enclosure in the observation point'
findings.quote: Nasar (et al. 1983) expected individuals 'to prefer more openness in a natural scene [and] more en-closure in the observation point' (Nasar et al. 356).

findings.antecedent: Understanding visual environment and its human affect
findings.quote: Nasar (1988) argued that a successful design results from understanding both the visual environment and its human affect.

findings.antecedent: Aesthetic quality of an environment
findings.consequent: Sense of being attracted to, distracted to, or repulsed by certain spatial conditions, impacting well-being
findings.quote: The aesthetic quality of an environment influences the sense of being attracted to, or distracted to or repulsed by, certain spatial conditions which in turn have an impact on well-being.

findings.antecedent: Novel scenes (compared to familiar scenes)
findings.quote: Nasar assumed that relatively novel scenes would be preferred in comparison to relatively familiar scenes...

findings.antecedent: Visual complexity
findings.quote: ...and that preference was expected to be relative to visual complexity.

findings.antecedent: Environmental characteristics (light, open space, access to 'unambiguous refuge')
findings.quote: Environmental characteristics such as light, open space and access to an “unambiguous refuge” (323), by which they mean a space that has the potential for supporting human assistance if needed, are the indicators of safety.

findings.antecedent: Low ceiling plane
findings.quote: According to Hildebrand, a low ceiling plane is the most important dimension for creating a sense of containment (interior refuge).

findings.antecedent: Generous plan dimensions, significantly raised ceiling plane, increased light levels, generous expanses of transparent surface
findings.quote: Interior prospect, on the other hand, depends on “generous plan dimensions, a significantly raised ceiling plane, significantly increased light levels, and generous expanses of transparent surface” (1999, 32).

findings.antecedent: Moving from darker to lighter spaces
findings.quote: Furthermore, Hildebrand explains that when we move “from darker to lighter, we will again be able to see without being seen, and so will ensure for ourselves relative safety during exploration" (54).

findings.antecedent: High degree of order
findings.quote: He states that a high degree in order is associated with pleasure...

findings.antecedent: Balanced arrangement of prospect and refuge
findings.quote: The theory proposes that a balanced arrangement of prospect and refuge in an environment will achieve this affect.
